name: Root Certificate
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Certificate Nobody Else Signs
lesson.summary: A root certificate is self-signed and sits at the top of every certificate chain, meaning it is trusted not because a chain proves it but because it was installed into a trust store by decision rather than verification.
lesson.body:
Every certificate chain has to end somewhere. Walking up from a website's certificate to the intermediate that signed it eventually reaches a certificate that is not signed by anyone else at all. It is signed by its own private key, a property called self-signed, meaning the certificate's issuer field and subject field name the same entity, and it is called a root certificate. This is not a technical accident, it is a logical necessity. A signature chain that verifies signatures using the signer above it cannot go on forever, and it cannot verify its own starting point using the same method, because there is nothing above the top to check it against.

So how is a root certificate trusted at all, if not by verification? The honest answer is that it is trusted by decision, not by proof. Operating system vendors and browser makers maintain trust stores, curated lists of root certificates they have chosen to ship as trusted by default. Getting a root certificate authority added to a major trust store involves audits, published policies, and ongoing compliance reviews, but at the end of that process the root is trusted because a small number of organizations decided to include it, not because any cryptographic chain proves it deserves that trust. This is the point where the entire chain of digital signatures bottoms out into an act of institutional trust.

The practical consequences of this are significant. Because a root certificate's private key can sign an intermediate that can in turn sign a certificate for any domain, compromising a root key is one of the worst outcomes in the whole public key infrastructure. For this reason, root certificate authorities typically keep their signing keys offline entirely, stored in hardware security modules that never touch the internet, brought online only rarely and under strict procedural controls, sometimes involving multiple people who must jointly authorize any signing ceremony.

Consider what happens when a root certificate is removed from a trust store, which does occasionally happen when a certificate authority is found to have violated its obligations. Every certificate chain that terminates at that root, potentially millions of certificates issued by every intermediate beneath it, stops being trusted by any browser that removed the root, essentially overnight, forcing every affected website to obtain and install a new certificate from a still trusted authority. That single point of consequence is the flip side of the single point of convenience a root provides: one decision to trust it enables an entire tree of certificates below, and one decision to distrust it can invalidate that whole tree just as fast. This tension between convenience and concentrated risk is exactly what makes a root certificate function as what the next chapter calls a trust anchor.
